question: In community health, what do we mean by a non-human reservoir?

options.A: A medical facility designated strictly for treating infectious tropical diseases
options.B: A living or environmental source where a pathogen normally lives and multiplies
options.C: A pharmaceutical storage unit used to keep vaccines at very cold temperatures
options.D: A human patient who shows no active symptoms of a communicable illness

explanation: You've got this! Germs rely on reservoirs to survive and multiply in nature before they ever reach humans. Think of it as their permanent home base. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why are non-human reservoirs so important in the spread of diseases?

options.A: They purify local water sources so that waterborne parasites cannot infect people
options.B: They manufacture natural antibodies that help human populations fight off severe infections
options.C: They serve as temporary quarantine stations for individuals exposed to outbreaks
options.D: They provide a safe place for the infectious agent to survive and multiply over time

explanation: Spot on! Reservoirs act like safe breeding grounds for germs, making sure the disease cycle keeps going if we don't intervene. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h1)

question: Which animal is the main natural home for the Lassa fever virus here in Nigeria?
explanation: Great job! The multimammate rat sheds the Lassa virus in its waste, which can easily contaminate food items in our homes and barns. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h2)

question: A community health nurse is talking to abattoir (slaughterhouse) workers about their daily risks. Which animal-borne diseases should be the main focus?
explanation: You nailed it! Because abattoir workers handle livestock directly, they are at higher risk for zoonotic infections like anthrax and brucellosis. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h2)

question: What is the main goal of destroying a disease reservoir?

options.A: To eliminate the environmental or animal habitat where the pathogen survives
options.B: To provide permanent immunity to all human members of an affected community
options.C: To increase the population of beneficial predators that feed on disease vectors
options.D: To chemically alter drinking water supplies so they taste better to locals

explanation: Exactly! By taking away their home or habitat, we cut off the source of the infection entirely. Smart thinking! [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which of these is a good example of modifying the environment to control disease carriers?

options.A: Administering routine oral polio vaccines to newborn infants
options.B: Draining stagnant water pools where mosquitoes lay their eggs
options.C: Treating confirmed malaria patients with appropriate antimalarial drugs
options.D: Distributing insecticide-treated bed nets to pregnant mothers

explanation: Well done! Changing the physical surroundings—like clearing out standing water—stops mosquitoes from breeding there in the first place. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h3)

question: Which sanitation practice helps stop rats and mice from taking over residential areas?

options.A: Storing harvested grains directly on bare dirt floors inside homes
options.B: Properly covering refuse bins and clearing overgrown bushes
options.C: Leaving domestic food waste uncovered in open backyard spaces
options.D: Digging shallow soakaway pits close to kitchen entrances

explanation: Spot on! Covering trash cuts off their food supply, and clearing bushes takes away their hiding spots. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why is keeping our environment clean considered a primary defense against diseases?

options.A: It permanently alters the genetic makeup of pathogens so they become harmless
options.B: It ensures that community members never come into contact with wild animals
options.C: It replaces the need for any form of medical treatment during disease outbreaks
options.D: It removes the breeding grounds and shelter that vectors and pests need to survive

explanation: You got it! A clean environment denies pests the food, water, and shelter they need to multiply. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of vaccinating animals on a large scale in public health?

options.A: To cure animals that are already showing severe clinical signs of illness
options.B: To create a protective barrier that stops pathogens from spreading to humans
options.C: To increase the market weight and commercial value of livestock herds
options.D: To replace human vaccination schedules with veterinary immunization protocols

explanation: Exactly! Vaccinating animals keeps them healthy and stops zoonotic diseases from jumping over to humans. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h5)

question: If a local government wants to reduce rabies cases in humans, what should they prioritize first?

options.A: Draining all local ponds and slow-moving irrigation streams
options.B: Conducting a mass vaccination campaign for domestic dogs
options.C: Providing free insecticide-treated nets to market traders
options.D: Issuing strict travel bans on all livestock transport vehicles

explanation: Brilliant! Since dogs are the main carrier of rabies, vaccinating them directly protects us from exposure. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why is community involvement so important when trying to control disease reservoirs?

options.A: Community members are legally required to fund all government public health budgets
options.B: Local leaders must personally manufacture chemical pesticides and veterinary vaccines
options.C: Villagers need to conduct laboratory tests on captured rodents and vectors
options.D: Local residents must change daily habits like food storage and waste disposal for interventions to work

explanation: You're doing great! Public health measures only stick when everyday people change small daily habits to keep pests away. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which common practice puts people at high risk for Lassa fever by letting rodents touch food?

options.A: Keeping domestic cats inside the main living areas at night
options.B: Drying food crops out in the open on mats or bare ground
options.C: Storing clean drinking water inside tightly sealed plastic containers
options.D: Washing cooking utensils immediately after every family meal

explanation: Spot on! Leaving grains exposed outside invites infected rats to contaminate them with their urine and droppings. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h6)

question: What is a major challenge health workers face when trying to eradicate disease reservoirs?

options.A: Poor coordination between human health and veterinary agencies
options.B: Immediate compliance from all community members during campaigns
options.C: Excessive funding that leads to unspent public health budgets
options.D: An overabundance of trained environmental health personnel

explanation: That's right! Controlling animal-borne diseases needs teamwork between doctors and veterinarians, but communication gaps can slow things down. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h7)

question: During a suspected outbreak of an animal-borne disease, what is a key role for a nurse?

options.A: Manufacturing new chemical pesticides in a hospital laboratory
options.B: Reporting suspected cases and educating the community on prevention
options.C: Enforcing quarantine laws through police and military patrols
options.D: Designing blueprints for modern municipal drainage systems

explanation: You got it! Nurses are right on the front lines, helping catch outbreaks early and teaching people how to stay safe. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T6#GNS313_U2_T6_h7)
